docs.title: How the heat outlook is made
docs.what.p: Every morning the outlook collects the forecast runs of three families of global weather models for the next seven days: GFS from the United States, ICON from Germany and GEM from Canada. Each run is a slightly different but plausible version of the coming days. Together they show what is most likely and how sure we can be.
docs.correct.p: Global models are often a little too warm or too cool at one place. Every day the forecasts are compared with what the city's weather station measured, and the average difference of recent weeks is removed, separately for each model family.
docs.levels.hi: In Kaolack and Khulna the levels are based on the heat index, how hot it feels once humidity is taken into account. Each city has its own levels, Caution, Danger, Extreme and Critical, set for its climate.
docs.levels.lima: In Lima heat becomes a risk when both the day and the night stay unusually warm for the time of year, as in SENAMHI's heat wave definition. A level starts where the station's own record counts a day or a night as unusual for that date, and never below a fixed minimum for each level.
docs.rule.h: When a day gets a level
docs.rule.p: A day gets a level when at least 30 in 100 forecasts reach it, with each model family counting equally. The chance shown for each level is that share. In Lima, Danger and Extreme also need two of the three model families to agree.
docs.range.p: Eight in ten forecasts fall inside the likely range. The number on each day card is the middle forecast, the most likely value.
docs.later.h: Why later days are less certain
docs.later.p: The further ahead, the more the forecasts drift apart and the more often they miss. The first days are for acting, the later days for planning. Email alerts cover the first three days only, and the track record shows how well each lead time has done.
docs.official.p: The national weather services issue the official warnings: ANACIM in Senegal, BMD in Bangladesh and SENAMHI in Peru. When one is in force, the page shows it first. This outlook is local and experimental, and it can differ from a warning for a wider area. Follow the official warning.
docs.track.h: How the track record is scored
docs.track.p: Each forecast is compared with the measurement at the city's station once it is in. A hit is a day forecast at Danger or higher that was measured at Danger or higher. A miss is a day measured at Danger or higher that was forecast lower. A false alarm is a day forecast at Danger or higher that was measured lower.
docs.data.p: Each city's outlook is a public data file, updated every morning. It holds the seven days with their levels, chances and ranges, the official warning, and the verified history. Its format may still change, so please contact us before building on it.
docs.status.p: This outlook is a research forecast under test in Practical Action's Living in a Hotter World project, built by Meteory. It is not an official warning.
alert.title: Why each day got its level
alert.intro.machine: Every forecast day passes the same rules, in this order. Some rules look back: three hot days in a row, two runs agreeing, a dip of one day. Pick a day to follow it.
alert.intro.bands: Here the level comes from one rule: the share of the forecasts at each heat index level. Pick a day to see the numbers behind it.
alert.track.aria: The level day by day, with every rule that raised or lowered it
alert.track.note: A flat stretch keeps the level. Every arrow is a change: ▲ raises, ▼ lowers, and the number is the rule in the list below. The dot is the level shown that day. Click a day to see its rules.
alert.none: The steps for today's run are not available. The levels on the forecast page are unaffected.
alert.final: The level shown on the forecast page.
alert.s.nochange: The forecasts say {level}, and no rule changes it.
alert.s.persist: Three hot days in a row raise it to {level}.
alert.s.early: Early in the season it goes up to {level}.
alert.s.night: The nights are too cool, so it goes back to {level}.
alert.s.families: Not enough model families agree, so it comes down to {level}.
alert.s.agree: It waits for a second run, so {level} for now.
alert.s.dip: A dip of one day is held, so it stays at {level}.
alert.s.override: The country team sets it to {level}.
rule.persist: Three hot days in a row
rule.families: Two of three model families agree
rule.dip: A dip of one day is held
rule.test.text: Three hot days in a row, warm nights, two runs agreeing and dips of one day run in test here. They do not change the level yet.
rule.persist.moved: {n} forecasts had {min} or higher for {days} days running, counting the days the station measured before today. Each moves up one level. {pct}% now reach {level}.
rule.persist.none: No forecast has {min} or higher {days} days running yet.
rule.early.moved: {n} forecasts are early in the season and move up one level.
rule.early.none: Not early in the season, so no forecast moves up for that.
rule.night.moved.abs: {n} forecasts move back to {to}: {top} needs a warm following night.
rule.night.moved.pct: {n} forecasts move back to {to}: {top} needs a following night among the warmest {p} in 100 for this date at the station.
rule.night.none: No forecast has to move back for a cool night.
rule.night.unknown: For {n} forecasts the night after this day lies beyond the forecast, so they keep their level.
rule.families.held: {level} needs {n} of the 3 model families at {share}% on their own. Fewer agree, so the day comes down to {to}.
rule.families.ok: Enough model families agree, so the level stands.
rule.agree.off: Only days 5 to 7 wait for a second run.
rule.agree.held: Days 5 to 7 show {min} or higher only when two runs in a row agree. Yesterday's run had this day at {prev}, so it shows {to} until tomorrow's run confirms.
rule.agree.new: Days 5 to 7 show {min} or higher only when two runs in a row agree. Yesterday's run did not reach this day yet, so it shows {to} until tomorrow's run confirms.
rule.agree.ok: Yesterday's run also had this day at {min} or higher, so the level stands.
rule.agree.below: Below {min}, there is nothing to confirm.
rule.dip.off: Only today's level can be held through a dip.
rule.dip.held: Yesterday this day was at {yday}. Today's forecasts dip to {from}, but tomorrow is back at {tomorrow}, so the day keeps {to} through the dip.
rule.override.none: No override from the country team for this day.
